title: How Can We Measure the Causal Effects of Social Networks Using Observational Data? Evidence from the Diffusion of Family Planning and AIDS Worries in South Nyanza District, Kenya
venue: Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research (MPIDR) Working Paper WP 2001-022
design_class: observational (individual fixed-effects panel / linear probability model; OLS comparison)
exposure: number (and presence) of a woman's informal family-planning conversational-network partners who use contraception, measured prior to time t; also spatial/AIDS-worry network composition
outcome: probability a woman is currently using modern contraception (also ever-use, want-no-more-children, and own perceived AIDS risk)
effect_estimate: Individual fixed-effects LPM: probability of current contraceptive use rises by 'a little more than 0.038' per network partner who is a user on average; 'having one contraceptive user among the network partners increases the probability of the female respondent being a current user significantly by about 0.054'; each additional user beyond the first raises probability 'by about 0.032'. OLS estimate of the average per-user effect is biased upward by '180 percent' relative to FE. Effects are larger for men than for women.
effect_se_or_ci: n/a in text (point estimates significant; SEs/robust SEs reported in Table 5, not reproduced in narrative). One related regression: past use predicts 0.63 more current user-partners, t-ratio 4.43 in OLS, collapsing to ~0 with fixed effects.
direction: yes — more network partners who are contraceptive users RAISES the respondent's own probability of adopting/using contraception
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: partial — individual fixed effects sweep out time-invariant homophily/selection and fixed community unobservables (authors show OLS is upward-biased 180%), but there is no instrument or exogenous shock; identification rests on a maintained (untested) assumption that within-person changes in network composition are uncorrelated with period-specific random shocks, so time-varying common shocks are not fully excluded
setting_sample: Rural South Nyanza District, Nyanza Province, Kenya (Luo agro-pastoralists); Kenyan Diffusion and Ideational Change Project 3-wave longitudinal survey 1994/95, 1996/97, 2000; 497 women (324 men) present in all three waves used for family-planning FE estimates
routing_check: confirmed A.3 — person-to-person social diffusion of modern family planning through conversational networks, net of individual/community controls. Note: despite the methodological title it delivers an APPLIED fertility-control estimate (not method/theory only). Radio (A.20) and schooling are controls, not the diffusion channel of interest.
risk_of_bias: ROBINS-I overall: moderate — FE addresses selection/homophily and confounding by fixed traits (main strength); residual threats are time-varying confounding (period shocks), recall/systematic measurement error in reported networks, and sample attrition (authors test attrition, find little bias)
notes: Strongest-identified of the four A.3 PDFs. Best available FE estimates that social networks have a significant, substantial causal effect on contraceptive use (raising probability of use by ~one-third at sample means) and on AIDS-risk perception; effects nonlinear/asymmetric and larger for men. Applied, not merely methodological.

title: The Fertility Transition in Bavaria
venue: Yale University Economic Growth Center Discussion Paper No. 821
design_class: observational (county-level fixed-effects panel regression of marital fertility, 1880-1910, with IV for infant mortality using elevation and milch-cows-per-capita, and year dummies)
exposure: none direct for diffusion — the innovation/diffusion ('Princeton') hypothesis is tested only indirectly via whether year dummies ('time itself') retain explanatory power for marital fertility net of measured economic/social change; no measure of social/spatial exposure to prior adopters is constructed
outcome: index of marital fertility (Ig) / marital fertility rate at the county and urban-district level
effect_estimate: none reported for diffusion. Descriptive decline: overall Bavarian marital fertility fell ~19.6% 1880-1910 (rural ~11.5%, urban ~36.8%). Key finding against pure diffusion: once economic/social variables are included, the year dummies 'tell us nothing' — i.e., the residual time trend that diffusion theories rely on vanishes. Textile employment and rising female wages exert strong downward effects on fertility; Catholicism and secularization (SPD vote) matter; urbanization eventually lowers fertility.
effect_se_or_ci: n/a (elasticities and coefficients in Tables 3-4, not extracted; adjusted R-squared .94 rural, .79 urban)
direction: n/a — no social-diffusion exposure estimated; the paper argues economic/structural + cultural (religion/secularization) change, not diffusion, drives the transition
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: no — no diffusion exposure variable exists; the residual time/'simultaneity' effect that would proxy diffusion is precisely the common-shock/reflection confound, and the authors show it disappears once economic and social change are measured (evidence against, not for, a distinct diffusion effect)
setting_sample: Kingdom of Bavaria, Germany; 176 rural counties (Bezirksaemter) and urban districts; census years 1880, 1885, 1895, 1900, 1910; period 1880-1910 (broader descriptive series 1846-1912)
routing_check: confirmed A.3-relevant — an explicit econometric test/critique of the European Fertility Project (Princeton) innovation/diffusion interpretation of the fertility transition; bears directly on the A.3 hypothesis by rebutting the 'time itself'/diffusion residual. Provides no diffusion parameter of its own.
risk_of_bias: ROBINS-I overall (for the A.3 diffusion question): serious to critical — no diffusion measure; the reflection problem is not solved but rather shown to dissolve into measured economics. (The IV is for infant mortality, a control, not for diffusion.)
notes: This is the Princeton-tradition descriptive-residual case flagged in the brief: it works by asking whether the aggregate synchrony/time-effect that diffusion theory invokes survives better economic and social measurement, and finds it does not. Its contribution to A.3 is as counter-evidence to pure diffusion, not as an identified diffusion estimate. Identification of diffusion = no.

title: Social Transmission and the Spread of Modern Contraception in Rural Ethiopia
design_class: observational (discrete-time event-history hazard model with AIC-based model comparison / model averaging)
exposure: proportion of ever-users of modern contraception within a woman's (and her husband's) friendship network at time t-1 (unbiased and prestige-biased); minimum spatial distance to a contraceptive ever-user at t-1; network centrality (in/out-degree)
outcome: hazard of first-ever uptake of modern contraception (year of first use)
effect_estimate: Social-diffusion variables do NOT improve model fit: best model is individual factors + social environment (excludes network social-interaction terms; Akaike weight 0.29). Only a weak conditional interaction is detected: Parity x unbiased proportion of ever-users in women's network OR = 1.30. Non-interacted network exposure, spatial distance, and centrality are effectively null with high model uncertainty. By contrast individual/environment predictors are strong: parity OR = 1.43; education OR = 2.16; Orthodox Christian (vs Muslim) OR = 0.22; frequent radio use OR = 2.12.
effect_se_or_ci: Parity x prop.ever-users WNT: 95% CI [1.14; 1.51]. Comparators: parity [1.28;1.62]; education [1.53;3.03]; religion (Christian) [0.10;0.52]; radio [1.18;3.78]
direction: mixed/no — person-to-person social diffusion (friendship/spatial networks) does NOT robustly raise adoption; its role is marginal and only conditionally positive for high-parity women
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: no — cross-sectional survey-reconstructed networks; uses t-1 network composition to argue temporal ordering but has no instrument/exogenous variation and cannot separate genuine contagion from shared local conditions or homophily (authors themselves cite the Manski reflection problem and Shalizi-Thomas homophily-contagion confounding)
setting_sample: Community of agro-pastoralists in 4 villages, Arsi zone, southern rural Ethiopia; 936 ever-married women aged 15-52 surveyed 2008/9; adoption histories 1995-2008; contraceptive prevalence reached 18.8% by 2008
routing_check: confirmed A.3 — direct micro-level test of social transmission/diffusion of fertility control through friendship and spatial networks. Radio (A.20 media) and religion (A.6/D.1) enter only as controls; the A.3 diffusion channel is the object of study and is found marginal.
risk_of_bias: ROBINS-I overall: serious — reflection/homophily confounding unaddressed, recall-based retrospective adoption dates, censored/incomplete network data, association-only. (Result is a well-executed but non-identified micro test.)
notes: IMPORTANT: this file is titled 'Correction:...' but the PDF is the COMPLETE standalone article carrying all data, tables and results (not a content-free erratum) — usable as a full study. A rare 'first-cases' micro-diffusion test whose honest conclusion is that person-to-person diffusion contributes little to early contraceptive uptake once individual and religious/media factors are controlled; phenomenon is a contemporary (post-1965) developing-country early transition, coded SDT by era though structurally an FDT-type onset.

title: Playing the Fertility Game at Work: An Equilibrium Model of Peer Effects
venue: MPRA Paper No. 45914 (Munich Personal RePEc Archive); working paper, March 2013
design_class: structural/simulation (game-theoretic Nash-equilibrium peer-effects model with multiple equilibria, estimated via Ciliberto-Tamer partial-identification bounds; establishment/firm random effects for common shocks; sister-fertility exclusion restriction; individual Probit as reduced-form benchmark)
exposure: number (or share) of a woman's fertile-aged female coworkers at the same work establishment who have a child in the period (endogenous peer fertility)
outcome: probability of / number of women having a child (indicator for a birth between Dec 2002 and Nov 2005)
effect_estimate: Naive individual Probit: each additional coworker with a child raises own fertility propensity ~1.0 pp (basic), ~0.3 pp with individual controls, ~0.5 pp with contextual controls, positive and significant. Full structural model with firm/establishment random effects: sign REVERSES to negative average peer effects; turning on (homogeneous) peer effects yields a '5-percentage point decline' in the share predicted to have a child. Heterogeneous model: positive across worker types defined by age/education, but negative within age groups and among low-education women (who dominate the sample). Reported as parameter BOUNDS, not point estimates; equilibrium selection matters: two-type-by-education average peer combination changes fertility by +25 pp (highest-fertility equilibrium) vs -7.5 pp (lowest); ~40-50% of workplaces have multiple equilibria.
effect_se_or_ci: n/a — partially identified; 95% confidence parameter bounds reported in Tables 4/6/7 (not point estimates or SEs)
direction: mixed — negative average/homogeneous peer effect once common shocks are absorbed (more coworker childbearing LOWERS own childbearing), but positive within some subgroups and across types; net sign depends on model and equilibrium selection
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: partial — the structural game plus firm/establishment random effects explicitly absorb workplace common shocks (naive positive effect flips to negative when they are added), and a sister-fertility exclusion restriction separates endogenous from contextual effects; but effects are only set-identified (bounds), residual peer self-selection/sorting into workplaces is only partly tested (public vs private sector), and the mechanism is a mix of economic (career competition, replacement/scale diseconomies) and social (conformity) channels
setting_sample: Denmark; merged administrative employer-employee + fertility register; fertile-aged women (20-40) working in medium establishments (10-50 employees) as of Nov 2002; 151,494 women across 31,725 establishments; birth outcomes 2003-2005
routing_check: confirmed A.3-adjacent (social-interaction/peer-effects evidence on fertility) but FLAG mechanism mismatch: the peer effect concerns the decision to HAVE a child among coworkers, driven substantially by economic channels (labor-market competition, leave/replacement costs) as much as social conformity — it is NOT specifically diffusion/social-learning of fertility CONTROL knowledge or acceptability. Borderline with A.3's core parameter; largest signal is workplace/career, not contraceptive diffusion.
risk_of_bias: n/a (theory/structural) for the modelling core; for its applied Danish estimates, ROBINS-I overall: moderate — strong design against common shocks and reflection, but only partial identification (bounds), possible residual sorting, and mixed/uninterpretable mechanism
notes: One of the two method/structural papers. It DOES deliver an applied fertility estimate (Danish register data), so it is not theory-only. Central methodological lesson relevant to A.3: naive peer-fertility correlations are positive but reverse to negative once workplace common shocks are absorbed — a clean illustration of the reflection/common-shock problem. Multiple equilibria and partial identification mean no single point estimate exists.

title: Residential segregation and the fertility of immigrants and their descendants
design_class: observational — hierarchical (multilevel) Poisson log-linear model with random Local-Authority intercepts on linked longitudinal census + birth-register data; no exogenous variation, but childhood community composition is measured before childbearing to remove reverse causation/simultaneity
exposure: childhood community population composition / residential segregation, measured in the 1971 census (before childbearing): (a) size and (b) proportion of foreign-born or same-country-of-birth-group population in the Local Authority, and (c) ward-level index of dissimilarity, each ranked into top 5% / 5-25% / bottom 75% (top 2% / 3-5% / bottom 95% for South Asians)
outcome: completed fertility (total children born to each woman by 2009)
effect_estimate: All migrants (Table 2, IRR vs ancestral natives=1.0): child migrants raised in top-5% most foreign-born LAs IRR 1.14*** (size, Model A1); index-of-dissimilarity top 5% IRR 1.25*** (Model A5, ~25% more children than natives); least-segregated migrants not significantly different from natives. Pakistani/Bangladeshi (Table 3): top-2% size IRR 1.61*** (first gen), 1.57*** (second gen); index of dissimilarity top 40% IRR 1.75***. Indian (Table 4): top-2% size IRR 1.28**. Higher segregation/co-ethnic concentration in childhood -> higher completed fertility (i.e., less exposure to the native low-fertility norm).
effect_se_or_ci: SEs reported. Table 2: A1 top 5% SE 0.03; A5 top 5% SE 0.06. Table 3 (Pak/Bangladeshi): top 2% size SE 0.16 (1st gen), 0.13 (2nd gen); IoD top 40% SE 0.15. Table 4 (Indian): top 2% SE 0.10. Significance stars: *p<.05, **p<.01, ***p<.001.
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: no — no exogenous variation in segregation; it is a multilevel association. The childhood-exposure design removes reverse causation and simultaneity (exposure measured before the woman's own childbearing) but does not separate true socialisation/diffusion from parental residential selection into co-ethnic areas or common cultural shocks; authors concede community composition as norm-exposure is a construct-validity assumption and flag the modifiable areal unit problem.
setting_sample: England & Wales; ONS Longitudinal Study (1% sample) linked 1971-2009; women under 16 in 1971 followed to completed fertility in 2009; N=50,152 (44,168 ancestral natives, 1,074 first-generation child migrants, 4,910 second generation), with a South Asian (Pakistani/Bangladeshi, Indian) focus.
routing_check: confirmed A.3 — Wall-1 residential-segregation paper whose estimand is diffusion of fertility norms: it tests the childhood-socialisation hypothesis, treating segregation as a diffusion-limiting social structure that governs childhood exposure to the native low-fertility norm versus the origin-culture high-fertility norm (‘cultural entrenchment’). This is diffusion-of-fertility-behaviour content, not pure composition, and not a content-agnostic channel (so not A.20).
risk_of_bias: serious — confounding: residual selection from parents sorting into co-ethnic/segregated neighbourhoods on unobserved fertility preferences, plus construct-validity of composition as a proxy for norm exposure and the modifiable areal unit problem; the childhood-timing design is a genuine strength that removes reverse causation but provides no exogenous variation.
notes: All estimates are full-text (Tables 2-4), not abstract-only. Methodologically careful (completed fertility, pre-childbearing exposure, multiple composition measures giving consistent results), and the strongest observational design of the segregation pair, but still unidentified in the diffusion-vs-common-shock sense. Findings support the childhood-socialisation / diffusion reading: fertility of immigrants is closer to native fertility when they grow up in less segregated areas.

title: Spillovers in Childbearing Decisions and Fertility Transitions: Evidence from China
venue: Tinbergen Institute Discussion Paper TI 2020-031/V (working paper)
design_class: quasi-experimental (partial-population experiment; IV with DiD/event-study support). Instrument = Han policy-exposure (ER) x local Han share; endogenous regressor = leave-me-out reference-group mean completed fertility
exposure: reference-group average completed fertility of peers (women in same prefecture, same hukou, same birth cohort); peer exposure driven by Han family-planning-policy shock interacted with local Han share
outcome: completed fertility (children ever born) of ethnic-minority women
effect_estimate: IV estimate theta = 0.648 (Table 4, col 3): a minority woman gives birth to 0.65 fewer children when her reference-group average completed fertility is exogenously reduced by one child. Reduced-form Han-share x Exposure coefficient = -0.193 (Table 4, col 1). Direct Han policy effect (Han sample) rho = -0.22 births per one-birth expected reduction.
effect_se_or_ci: theta: SE 0.102, 95% CI [0.45, 0.85]; reduced-form -0.193 SE 0.041; both significant at 1%; first-stage F > 100 (=103.1)
direction: yes — a peer (reference-group) reduction in fertility causally lowers a woman's own fertility (social multiplier); indirect/spillover component is ~one third of total policy effect
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: yes — exogenous variation from staggered LLF-campaign rollout across provinces and cohorts (Han were subject to quotas, minorities exempt) interacted with local Han share; parallel pre-trends shown via event study and placebo test on older cohorts, and confounders (Great Famine, Cultural Revolution, Send-down movement) explicitly controlled
setting_sample: China, 1970s-1980s family-planning era; 1% sample of 1990 census, cohorts born 1926-1945 (women aged 45-64); 57,570 minority and 726,907 Han women
routing_check: confirmed A.3 — provides an identified estimate of a peer/spillover (social-multiplier) effect on fertility; note the authors decompose it into a SOCIAL (conformism) channel and an ECONOMIC (quantity-quality / equilibrium price of a child) channel, and explicitly test and rule out 'social learning about birth control' as the mechanism, so part of theta is economic rather than pure social diffusion
risk_of_bias: low to moderate — strong quasi-experimental design with rich robustness (event study, placebo, confounding-shock controls); main residual threat is the non-testable exclusion restriction (that Han-share x exposure affects minority fertility only through peer mean fertility, e.g. imperfect enforcement of minority exemptions), which the authors address but cannot fully prove
notes: Full-text working paper with complete regression tables (Table 4). theta stable across specifications: 0.65 baseline, 0.63 controlling ER directly, 0.55 in most conservative spec, 0.74 in the 12-cohort placebo-matched sample. Phenomenon coded FDT because this is China's first (marital) fertility transition from high to low deliberate-control fertility, but note the calendar timing (1970s) falls inside the review's SDT window rather than the 1870-1965 FDT window.

title: Social interactions, ethnicity, religion, and fertility in Kenya
design_class: structural/econometric GMM social-interactions model (Manski endogenous/exogenous/correlated decomposition made non-linear via Poisson/GMM) with quasi-experimental IV — mean rainfall and rainfall seasonality (District Rainfall Seasonality index) instrument the endogenous conformist effect
exposure: two diffusion terms: (1) endogenous conformist effect = deviation of own children-ever-born from the mean CEB of other women in the same village cluster / ethnic group (social contagion in fertility norms); (2) exogenous interaction = mean education of other women in the cluster; plus ethnicity and religion group membership
outcome: children ever born (CEB) / completed fertility (analysis restricted to women aged 30-49)
effect_estimate: Endogenous conformist effects positive and significant (Table 8, spec III, coefficient with IRR): Kikuyu 0.237*** (IRR 1.267), Kamba 0.221** (1.247), Kalenjin 0.190** (1.209), Luhya 0.179* (1.196), Kissi 0.159*** (1.172), Luo 0.123* (1.131) — i.e. a one-unit rise in the group-mean fertility deviation raises expected CEB by ~13-27%. Ethnic effects (Table 8 III) relative to Kikuyu: Luo 0.279** (1.321), Luhya 0.240** (1.272), Kalenjin 0.200** (1.221). Exogenous (ethnic-level education) effects mostly insignificant.
effect_se_or_ci: Reported as p-values under each coefficient (not SEs). Conformist effects (Table 8 III): Kikuyu p=0.000, Kamba p=0.003, Kalenjin p=0.003, Luhya p=0.011, Kissi p=0.000, Luo p=0.049. Standard errors robust to intra-cluster correlation. Overidentification: J-stat 7.803 (p=0.253) Table 8, 7.493 (p=0.278) Table 10 (pass); religion-only model J=19.046 (p=0.004) fails.
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: partial — the paper explicitly confronts Manski's reflection problem and separates the endogenous social-interaction (conformist) effect from exogenous/correlated effects using (a) the non-linearity of the Poisson/GMM conditional mean and (b) rainfall mean & seasonality as excluded instruments, validated with a J-test; identification still rests on functional-form and the exclusion restriction (rainfall may affect fertility through income/agriculture beyond the modeled channel).
setting_sample: Kenya, 1998 Kenya DHS (TFR ~4.7); 5,994 rural women aged 15-49 (completed-fertility analysis restricted to 30-49) across 6 main ethnic groups and 3 religions; matched to 1930-2000 monthly rainfall from 31 meteorological stations.
routing_check: confirmed A.3 — core estimand is the social-interaction/social-learning effect of socially proximate others' fertility (village-cluster and ethnic-group peers) on own completed fertility; the endogenous conformist effect is precisely peer adoption raising/lowering own fertility. Not A.20 (models the substantive fertility norm, not a content-agnostic media/network-architecture channel); religion (A.6/D.1-adjacent) effects tested and found largely insignificant, so it is not primarily a religion paper.
risk_of_bias: moderate — main threat: identification of the endogenous effect relies on the rainfall exclusion restriction and on non-linear functional form; residual confounding/correlated effects possible, and the religion specification fails the overidentification test (though the ethnicity specifications pass).
notes: All estimates are full-text (Tables 8-10). This is the strongest-identified of the three PDFs: it directly targets the reflection problem with an instrument. Kikuyu (lowest-fertility group) show the strongest endogenous/conformist effect, consistent with social multipliers sustaining a low-fertility norm; conformity is symmetric (amplifies whichever norm prevails), hence direction coded mixed. Coefficients are proportional changes in CEB; IRRs shown in tables.

title: Segregation, fertility, and son preference: the case of the Roma in Serbia
design_class: observational (OLS on number of children + Cox proportional-hazard model of birth spacing; no exogenous/quasi-experimental variation in segregation)
exposure: residential segregation of Roma settlements, coded categorically as only Roma / mostly Roma / few Roma (interpreted as exposure to the low-fertility Serbian majority culture and thus to cultural diffusion of the small-family and son-preference norms)
outcome: marital/completed fertility (number of living children, intensive margin); also birth-spacing hazard and sex ratio at last birth (son preference)
effect_estimate: Descriptive: households in 'few Roma' settlements have ~0.8 fewer children (Table 1: 2.811 vs 3.581 in 'only Roma'). OLS baseline (Table 2, col 1): few Roma -0.791*** children, mostly Roma -0.341*; with full controls (col 7): few Roma -0.459***, mostly Roma -0.215**. Birth spacing (Table 3, Panel B, col 1): few Roma coefficient -0.449*** on subsequent-birth hazard (~36% less likely to have an extra child). Son preference: 'few Roma-male' spacing coefficient -0.604* (Table 4).
effect_se_or_ci: OLS col 1: few Roma SE 0.189, mostly Roma SE 0.185; col 7: few Roma SE 0.140, mostly Roma SE 0.094. Hazard Table 3 col 1: few Roma SE 0.156. Table 4 few Roma-male SE 0.260. Robust SEs clustered at settlement level with Moulton confidence intervals.
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: no — authors explicitly state segregation 'does not stem from quasi-experimental variation' and that they 'do not estimate causal effects'; the diffusion interpretation is a descriptive residual (controls shrink but do not close the gap), and selection/common-cause confounding is conceded.
setting_sample: Belgrade, Serbia; primary survey Fall 2010; 300 Roma households across 13 settlements (with MICS 2010 non-Roma Serb comparison); women observed at intensive margin.
routing_check: confirmed A.3 — Wall-1 residential-segregation paper, but its estimand is genuinely diffusion-of-fertility-control content: segregation is framed as a diffusion-limiting social structure governing exposure to the Serbian majority's low-fertility and son-preference norms, and the paper documents cultural transmission (not just composition). Not A.20 (content is the norm itself, not a content-agnostic channel).
risk_of_bias: serious — confounding: no exogenous variation in segregation and self-acknowledged omitted-variable/common-shock confounding; also selection (sample trimmed of most desegregated households, non-representative).
notes: All estimates are full-text (Tables 1-4), not abstract-only. Authors' own framing is associational, not causal. Mechanism evidence for diffusion is indirect: less-segregated Roma both have lower fertility and stronger son preference matching the surrounding Serbs, which they read as cultural assimilation from majority to minority. Useful as suggestive/descriptive support for A.3 but must be graded as unidentified.

title: Diffusion Test of Fertility Decline in Arab Countries of the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) Region
venue: Journal of Population and Social Studies (JPSS), Vol. 30, pp. 562-590
design_class: descriptive (spatiotemporal Knox statistic with 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations; supported by a random-effects panel regression to impute the Ig marital-fertility index)
exposure: spatiotemporal proximity of countries — Knox pairing of geographic closeness (shared border or centroid distance < first quartile, 1,130 km) with temporal closeness (onset of fertility decline in the same 5-year period)
outcome: onset/timing of marital fertility decline dated two ways: Schmertmann et al. 2010 method on TFR (SA) and Coale & Treadway 1986 method on Coale's Ig marital-fertility index (CT)
effect_estimate: none reported (no effect size). The paper reports two Knox test results only: CT method p-value = 0.3796 (contingency 9/18/36/90); SA method p-value = 0.0549 (contingency 8/8/37/100)
effect_se_or_ci: n/a (Knox test p-values via Monte Carlo; no coefficient, SE, or CI)
direction: mixed — CT method finds NO significant spatiotemporal clustering (contagion rejected, p=0.38); SA method finds weak clustering significant only at the 6% level (p=0.055)
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: no — a Knox spatiotemporal-clustering test cannot separate true contagion from a common regional shock; the authors themselves state spatiotemporal interaction is only evidence 'if it is not explained by the spatiotemporal patterns of other relevant variables', and they fall back on descriptive 'favorable context' / elite-first narrative (a descriptive-residual argument)
setting_sample: 18 Arab MENA countries, fertility transition c. 1965-2019; UN World Population Prospects estimates 1950-2025, supplemented for pre-1970 nuptiality
routing_check: confirmed A.3 — the paper's explicit aim is to test whether the MENA marital-fertility decline resulted from spatiotemporal diffusion (contagion) of deliberate birth control among countries
risk_of_bias: serious — inconclusive/contradictory results across the two dating methods; ecological country-level analysis with no control for common economic/cultural determinants (confounding); arbitrary spatial-proximity thresholds; cannot rule out simultaneous common shocks
notes: Full-text article; all numeric content is descriptive (Knox p-values in Tables 3-4, onset dates in Tables 1-2, Ig maps in Fig 4). No usable causal effect size. Conclusion is agnostic: authors say the decline was EITHER contagious (SA) OR an intrinsic within-country social/vertical diffusion led by urban elites (CT); they lean on contextual descriptives (elites/cities transitioning first). Phenomenon coded FDT as MENA's first marital-fertility transition, but the calendar timing (1965-2019) lies in the review's SDT window.

title: Bring a Friend: Strengthening Women's Social Networks and Reproductive Autonomy in India
venue: IZA Discussion Paper No. 15381 (working paper); study registered AEARCTR-0003283
design_class: RCT — individual-level stratified randomization into 3 arms (control n=350; 'Own' voucher n=156; 'Bring-a-Friend' (BAF) voucher n=165); OLS on endline outcomes with village fixed effects
exposure: randomized inducement to expand/strengthen female peer social ties: the BAF voucher lets a woman offer accompanying female peers their own FP voucher (peer-engagement treatment), benchmarked against the 'Own' voucher (financial access only). Clean social-network parameter = BAF minus Own
outcome: modern contraceptive adoption (also: FP clinic visits, number of close peers in village, FP-related peer engagement, fear of stigma)
effect_estimate: Modern contraceptive use rose 6 percentage points for both voucher arms vs control (a 56% increase over the 12% control mean). BAF vs Own difference not significant on average (peer effect significant only in subgroups facing social barriers, e.g. +11 p.p. for women valuing concealability). BAF expanded close peers in village by 0.13 (21% over control mean 0.64) and cut fear of stigma by 38%.
effect_se_or_ci: 6 p.p. contraceptive effect NOT significant at conventional levels: p-values 0.116 (Own) and 0.106 (BAF). Close-peers +0.13 and stigma -38% reported as significant (SEs not transcribed from tables; robust SEs, robust to village clustering and wild-cluster bootstrap)
direction: yes (for adoption) — voucher access raises modern-contraceptive adoption; the incremental peer-support (BAF) channel raises adoption/network size only for socially constrained subgroups
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: yes — randomized assignment eliminates the reflection/common-shock problem by design; the BAF-vs-Own contrast cleanly isolates the peer-network channel net of the financial (voucher) channel
setting_sample: Rural India, Jaunpur district, Uttar Pradesh; 671 married women aged 18-30, 28 villages; 10-month intervention, baseline 2018
routing_check: confirmed A.3 for the BAF-vs-Own contrast (identified peer/social-network channel raising contraceptive adoption net of the FP program), but blended with A.5 (the voucher IS a family-planning-program subsidy and drives the headline 6 p.p. / 56% adoption effect) and A.6 (measures fear-of-stigma, cut 38% by BAF). The pooled contraceptive headline is the A.5 voucher effect, not the A.3 peer effect.
risk_of_bias: moderate — well-conducted registered RCT with balance checks and Lee bounds; but statistically underpowered (headline contraceptive effect only marginally significant, p~0.11; peer effect significant only in subgroups), small cluster count (28 villages), and some baseline imbalance in mother-in-law opposition and baseline FP use
notes: Full-text working paper. Note the mechanism is peer accompaniment/support to physically access an FP clinic and overcome mother-in-law opposition (instrumental social support), NOT the informational/normative social learning about the acceptability of limiting births that A.3 centrally describes; the paper does not measure peer adoption -> own adoption. Study is on contemporary unmet-need FP access, hence SDT-era developing-country context.
